records.place: Mainqué, Alto Valle del Río Negro, Patagonia

wine.name: Treinta y Dos Pinot Noir
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir alone, from ungrafted vines planted in 1932.
wine.sites: The old vineyard planted in 1932 that the house took on in 2004, a small plot at Mainqué in the Alto Valle on layered clay, sand and pebbles, on its own roots and farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts and little intervention, mostly in concrete vats. The wine is then aged in a mix of large concrete vats and old French oak barrels with little new wood, for nine months to two years by vintage, and about a year and a half in many.
wine.glass: Pale ruby; crushed raspberry, wild strawberry, red cherry and rose over rosehip and a stony, almost tile like note; light in body and taut, with gentle, fine grained tannin, bright acidity and a long, fine finish.
wine.ageing: Pretty when young, it has the structure to keep, and a strong vintage gains for ten years and more.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, a short airing will do; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: Spanish for thirty two: the year 1932, when the vineyard was planted, not a vintage.
The single grape of the wine, from the vines planted in 1932.
The river valley of northern Patagonia where the vineyard lies, low, dry and windy.

records.table: Treinta y Dos is Bodega Chacra's Pinot Noir from an ungrafted vineyard at Mainqué, in the Río Negro valley, planted in 1932 and named for that year. Pale, taut and scented with raspberry and rose, it wants a Burgundy glass and a cool cellar temperature.
records.story: Pinot Noir was planted at Mainqué, in the Alto Valle of the Río Negro, in 1932, and it stayed on its own roots: the valley's dry air, sandy soils and steady wind are often said to have kept phylloxera away. By the turn of the century the vineyard had been abandoned and gave little fruit. A member of the Tuscan family behind Sassicaia came to the valley, worked a vintage beside a Danish winemaker there, and in 2004 took on the old vineyard; one account says its owner tried to talk him out of it, so little did the vines yield. His first commercial wine, of the 2004 vintage, was named Treinta y Dos, thirty two, for the year of planting. Two more old Pinot Noir sites followed, one planted in 1955, which gave Cincuenta y Cinco, and one of 1967, and a new block was later planted with cuttings from the vines of 1932 and 1955. From the start the house farmed biodynamically, making its preparations from the plants and animals of its own estate. Treinta y Dos showed that Argentina had a Pinot Noir of old vines and fine bones, far from Mendoza and its Malbec, and it remains the bottle that makes that argument.

others.name: Cincuenta y Cinco
others.note: Pinot Noir from the vineyard planted in 1955, the companion of Treinta y Dos.

others.name: Barda
others.note: The house's entry Pinot Noir, the bottle a guest is most likely to meet first.

others.name: Mainqué Chardonnay
others.note: The house's white, aged partly in oak and partly in amphora.

traps: Treinta y Dos names the year 1932, when its vines were planted, not a vintage; Cincuenta y Cinco names 1955 in the same way.
Chacra grows in the low, windy Río Negro valley of Patagonia, where the cool comes from latitude, not in the high altitude vineyards of Mendoza.
Chacra shares a family with Sassicaia, but it is a separate house and makes no Bolgheri wine.

cards.back: The year 1932, when its ungrafted Pinot Noir vineyard at Mainqué was planted.

questions.q: A guest asks how the vines behind Chacra's Treinta y Dos survived on their own roots. Which answer fits?
opts: Dry air, sandy soils and wind kept phylloxera away
They were grafted onto American rootstock in 1932
Altitude above two thousand metres kills the louse
The vines were replanted from cuttings every decade
questions.exp: The Alto Valle's dry climate, sandy soils and steady wind are credited with keeping phylloxera out, so the 1932 vines stand ungrafted; the valley is low, not high.

questions.q: Which year gives Bodega Chacra's flagship Pinot Noir its name?
questions.exp: Treinta y Dos means thirty two, for the planting of 1932; 1955 is the vineyard behind Cincuenta y Cinco, and 2004 the house's first vintage.

report: Founded 2004 agrees with the library; the house's press kit gives 2004 as the first commercial release, while a 2008 and a 2010 article call 2006 the first vintage, and some sources say the house was set up in 2003.
Sources differ on whether the 1932 vineyard was leased or bought in 2004, so the record says the house took it on.
The size of the vineyard is given as two and as two and a half hectares; the sites field says a little over two.
The barrel time varies by vintage from nine months (2020) to twenty four (2012), with eighteen or nineteen in a general account, so the making gives the range.
The first release's case count is left out as a production figure; the 1967 vineyard's own wine is not named for want of a source.
The Danish winemaker and the founder are living and are not named.

records.place: General Roca, Alto Valle del Río Negro, Patagonia

wine.name: Old Vineyard Sémillon
wine.sites: The Finca Milagros vineyard in the Alto Valle near General Roca, planted with Sémillon in 1942 and farmed for its old vines.
wine.making: Pressed gently and fermented cool, with native yeasts by the house's account. Part of the wine is fermented in oak, about a fifth in new barrels in the 2022 vintage, and the rest kept in tank, so the wood shows only as a touch of vanilla.
wine.glass: Fig, ripe melon and green apple over honeysuckle and honey, with a touch of coconut and vanilla from the oak; a waxy, rounded texture held by lively acidity.
wine.ageing: Fresh and fruity in its first years, it gains honey and a waxy depth with five years or so in bottle, as old vine Sémillon does.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass of medium size.

label.means: The house's range from its old vines, a tribute to the first vineyards of the valley; some labels read Old Vine.
The vineyard named on later labels, planted with Sémillon in 1942.
The house, named for the engineer who founded it at General Roca in 1909.

records.table: Old Vineyard Sémillon is Humberto Canale's white from Sémillon planted in 1942 in the Finca Milagros vineyard near General Roca. Fig, melon and honeysuckle over a waxy texture and lively acidity: pour it cool, beside fish or white meat.
records.story: Humberto Canale was a civil engineer who came to Buenos Aires from Genoa, and in 1909, by his family's account brought south by one of his engineering professors, he chose the Alto Valle of the Río Negro near General Roca for a vineyard. The valley had only lately been opened to settlers after the Conquest of the Desert, and irrigation from the river was turning dry land into farms. Canale is credited with bringing the grapes that would mark the house, Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Sémillon among them, and the winery he founded is counted among the oldest in Argentine Patagonia. It has stayed in his family ever since: the line of his great nephews, the Barzi family, has run it for generations. In 1942 Sémillon was planted in the vineyard called Finca Milagros, and those vines feed the Old Vineyard range, which the house presents as a tribute to the first vineyards of the valley, planted more than eighty years ago. The white matters because it is old vine Sémillon from a valley better known for apples and pears and, lately, for Pinot Noir: a wine that carries the long memory of the Alto Valle in a glass.

others.name: Old Vineyard Riesling
others.note: A Riesling of the same old vine range, from the Alto Valle.

traps: Humberto Canale is in Río Negro, at General Roca in the Alto Valle, not in Neuquén's San Patricio del Chañar.
Labels and merchants give both Old Vine and Old Vineyard Sémillon, at times with Finca Milagros: one wine of the house's old vine range.

report: The house's own domain gave no search results, so every fact rests on two secondary sources.
The founding is 1909 in every source read save one merchant's 1914 and one note of first vineyards in 1912; the record uses 1909.
The founder's dates were not found, so he is named without them and described as a civil engineer from Genoa; flag for the refuter, who may find them or ask that the name be dropped.
The planting year 1942 rests on two merchants and Forbes Argentina; La Nación's headline speaks of vineyards of 1937, which may be another block.
The share of new oak is the 2022 figure from one merchant; the other confirms only partial oak.

The Gran Reserva Malbec, a Pinot Noir and the Estate 1909 Merlot the plan names were not found in two sources, so others carries the Riesling alone; the professor who brought the founder south is not named for want of a second source.

records.place: Mainqué, Alto Valle del Río Negro, Patagonia

wine.name: Noemía
wine.grapes: Malbec alone, from ungrafted vines planted in 1932.
wine.sites: A small single vineyard at Mainqué in the Alto Valle, planted in 1932 on its own roots and farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented with native yeasts, in some vintages in large open oak vats with a share of whole bunches and in others in concrete and egg shaped tanks. It is then aged for about eighteen months, from fifteen to twenty three by vintage, mostly in large casks of 600 litres, with new barriques in some years.
wine.glass: Blackberry, black cherry and dark currant over rose petal, mint and a stony note; creamy and full yet fresh, with fine, ripe tannin and a long finish.
wine.ageing: Generous when young, it keeps its fruit and fine tannin for a decade and more in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's name as the label prints it, Bodega Noemía of the Río Negro valley.
The single grape of the wine, from the vines of 1932.
The river valley of northern Patagonia, low, dry and windy, where the vineyard lies.

records.table: Noemía is Bodega Noemía's flagship Malbec, from ungrafted vines planted in 1932 at Mainqué in the Río Negro valley. Dark fruited and creamy, lifted by rose petal and mint, it wants a decanter for an hour and a Bordeaux glass.
records.story: Malbec was planted at Mainqué, in the Alto Valle of the Río Negro, in 1932, and the little vineyard stayed on its own roots as the decades passed. As the house tells it, an Italian countess and a Danish winemaker who were working in the valley came upon the neglected plot, saw what it was, and bought the small property to make a little wine, almost for fun. Bodega Noemía was born of it in 2001. Each vine, the house says, is genetically distinct, a field of old Malbec rather than a single clone. The founders restored the vineyard and farmed it biodynamically, later with certification, and they built the rest of their range on grapes from growers of Mainqué, held on long leases. Noemía, from the vines of 1932, became the house's flagship, with J. Alberto and A Lisa beneath it. The wine changed how Patagonian Malbec was seen: dense and dark, yet with the freshness and fine bones of a cool, windy and low valley, rather than the sun of Luján de Cuyo or the altitude of the Uco Valley. Poured beside a Mendoza Malbec, it shows how far south the grape can travel and keep its poise.

others.name: J. Alberto
others.note: The house's second Malbec, beneath Noemía, from old vineyards of the valley.

others.name: A Lisa
others.note: A Malbec of the house from the Mainqué vineyards it leases, beneath J. Alberto.

traps: Noemía is both the house and its flagship Malbec; J. Alberto and A Lisa are its other wines, not a second estate.
Noemía grows in the low, windy Río Negro valley of Patagonia, not in the high Uco Valley of Mendoza.

cards.front: Bodega Noemía: when were the vines of its flagship Malbec planted?
cards.back: 1932, ungrafted, at Mainqué in the Alto Valle del Río Negro.

cards.front: In which year was Bodega Noemía born?
cards.back: 2001, in the Río Negro valley of northern Patagonia.

report: The plan's note recalls Valle Azul; the house's own site and the Decanter review put the 1932 vineyard at Mainqué, and one merchant ties Valle Azul only to a plot established in 2004, so the record says Mainqué.
The vineyard is given as 1.5 hectares by the house and 1.4 by Decanter; the record says about one and a half.

The first vintage from the 1932 vines is not settled: Decanter says the house was born in 2001 and one merchant that the first wine of 2001 was made from bought grapes and the vineyard bought in 2004, so the record gives only the founding.
The house's site dates the valley's canals to about two centuries ago, which seems too early for the Alto Valle; the claim is left out.
The order of the range, Noemía over J. Alberto over A Lisa, is the usual account but was not stated in two sources read; the J. Alberto vineyard of 1955 rests on one source and is left out.
Both founders are living and are not named.

records.place: San Patricio del Chañar, Neuquén, Patagonia

wine.name: Saurus Pinot Noir
wine.sites: The house's own vineyards around the winery at San Patricio del Chañar, in the irrigated desert of Neuquén.
wine.making: Part of the wine, about two fifths in the 2019 and 2023 vintages, is aged for nine months in oak barrels, French with some American in one vintage, and the rest is kept in stainless steel, so the oak shows only as a touch of vanilla.
wine.glass: Cherry, red plum and rose petal over forest floor and a touch of vanilla; medium in body, round and juicy, with fine, soft tannin and moderate acidity.
wine.ageing: Ready on release and made to be drunk young, it is at its freshest within a few years of the vintage.
wine.serve: 13 to 15 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a Burgundy glass.

label.means: The house's first range, named for the dinosaur found when its winery was built.
The name the range carries in Argentina; the house's first wine was a Saurus Select Pinot Noir.
The family house of San Patricio del Chañar, founded in 2001.

records.table: Saurus Pinot Noir is the red of Familia Schroeder's Saurus range, named for the dinosaur found as the winery was built at San Patricio del Chañar in Neuquén. Cherry, plum and rose, round and fresh, it is a Pinot Noir to pour a little cool.
records.story: Familia Schroeder was founded in 2001 by a businessman of a family of German origin, among the pioneers who planted vines in the irrigated desert of San Patricio del Chañar, in Neuquén. Early in the building of the winery the works turned up fossil bones: the remains of a plant eating dinosaur some seventy five million years old, by the house's account about twelve metres long. The family helped the palaeontologists through the long work of extraction, and when the species was described in 2010 it was named Panamericansaurus schroederi, for the Schroeder family and for the energy company that backed the dig. The house built a cellar over the place of the find, where the bones can be seen as they were found, and it named its first range of wines, and its restaurant, Saurus. Its first wine was a Saurus Select Pinot Noir of the 2003 vintage, and Pinot Noir became the grape the house is known for, made in several styles, a rosé among them. The Saurus Pinot Noir is the bottle a guest is most likely to meet on a list, and its story fits in a sentence: a Patagonian Pinot Noir from a cellar built over a dinosaur.

others.name: Saurus Estate Pinot Noir Rosé
others.note: A rosé of Pinot Noir in the Saurus Estate range of the house.

traps: Saurus is the house's range, named for a dinosaur; the house is Familia Schroeder, in Neuquén at San Patricio del Chañar, not in Río Negro.
Panamericansaurus schroederi is the dinosaur, named in 2010 for the family and an energy company; the wine range is simply Saurus.

All of it in new oak barrels for two years

questions.exp: Panamericansaurus schroederi was described in 2010; 2001 is the house's founding and 2003 the vintage of its first wine.

report: The plan leaves the pick open between the Saurus Pinot Noir and a Malbec; the house presents itself as a Pinot Noir specialist whose first wine was a Saurus Select Pinot Noir, so the record teaches the Pinot Noir.

Abroad the wine is sold as Saurus Pinot Noir and in Argentina as Saurus Select Pinot Noir; the two share the oak regime of about two fifths for nine months in barrel, so they are taken as one wine; the refuter may confirm.
The year of the fossil find is given as 2001, 2002 and June 2003 by different sources, so the story says early in the building of the winery; the naming of 2010 rests on Wikipedia and Wikispecies.
The founder's name is given by the house, but his dates were not found and he may be living, so he is described, not named.
The Familia Schroeder upper range the plan names was not found in two sources and is left out of others.

records.place: San Patricio del Chañar, Neuquén, Patagonia

wine.name: Special Blend
wine.grapes: Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon in roughly equal parts, with Merlot for the rest.
wine.sites: The house's vineyards at San Patricio del Chañar, planted from 1999 in the irrigated desert of Neuquén.
wine.making: Each grape is aged apart in French oak barrels for some months, about eight in one vintage, before the final blend is chosen; the blend then goes back to barrel for a second spell, more than a year in that vintage, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, cassis and dark cherry over liquorice, tobacco, dark chocolate and vanilla from the oak; full and ripe, with fine, soft tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Supple on release after its long time in oak, it keeps for a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant for an hour; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The house's flagship red, a blend of Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot.
Spanish for the end of the world, the house's name for its southern home.
The Patagonian province whose desert at San Patricio del Chañar the house planted from 1999.

records.table: Special Blend is Bodega del Fin del Mundo's flagship red, Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon with Merlot from San Patricio del Chañar in Neuquén, each grape aged apart in French oak before blending. Dark fruited and supple, it wants a decanter and red meat.
records.story: San Patricio del Chañar, north of the city of Neuquén, was dry steppe until the late 1990s, when river water was brought to the desert to plant vines on a large scale. Bodega del Fin del Mundo was founded there in 1999 by a businessman who saw a new wine region in the far south, and its first vineyards were planted that year. The first harvest came in 2002, and the house has made its wines at San Patricio del Chañar ever since, as the pioneer of the zone. Others followed it into the desert, Familia Schroeder among them, and the zone grew into the modern centre of Neuquén's wine, as the Alto Valle of the Río Negro is its historic one. The house planted the grapes of Bordeaux beside Malbec, and the Special Blend, a blend of Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, became its flagship, with vintages from 2003 onward. Each grape spends its first months in barrel on its own before the blend is chosen. The wine shows that Patagonia's desert, warm by day and cold by night, can ripen Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec into a deep red that keeps its freshness, a long way from the Bordeaux blends of Mendoza.

others.name: Fin del Mundo Gran Reserva
others.note: A red of the house's Gran Reserva level, beneath the Special Blend.

others.name: Fin del Mundo Reserva Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: A varietal Cabernet Sauvignon of the house's Reserva range.

traps: Bodega del Fin del Mundo is in Neuquén, at San Patricio del Chañar, not at the southern tip of Argentina, whatever its name suggests.
The Special Blend is a blend of Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot, not a varietal Malbec.

cards.front: Bodega del Fin del Mundo: which grapes make its Special Blend?
cards.back: Malbec and Cabernet Sauvignon in roughly equal parts, with Merlot.

cards.front: In which year did Bodega del Fin del Mundo make its first harvest?
cards.back: 2002, after its first vines were planted at San Patricio del Chañar in 1999.

questions.q: A guest asks how the Special Blend of Bodega del Fin del Mundo is put together. Which answer fits?
opts: Each grape is aged apart in oak, then blended and returned to barrel
The grapes are fermented together in one vat and bottled young
Malbec alone is aged in old casks for five years
The wine is blended from purchased Mendoza wines
questions.exp: Malbec, Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot are aged apart in French oak before the blend is chosen, then the blend goes back to barrel; it is not a co-fermented young wine.

questions.q: In which year was Bodega del Fin del Mundo founded at San Patricio del Chañar?
questions.exp: The house was founded and planted its first vines in 1999, with a first harvest in 2002; 1909 is the founding of Humberto Canale in the Río Negro valley.

report: Founded 1999 rests on Mercado (founded in 1999) and ANBariloche (first plantings in 1999); the house's own site says it has made wine since 2002, the first harvest, which Wine Folly also gives.

Older labels read Special Blend Reserva and a 2019 listing Special Red Blend; the record uses Special Blend, the plan's words, and teaches the blend of about two fifths Malbec, two fifths Cabernet Sauvignon and a fifth Merlot that a critic's listings give for 2006, 2010 and 2019 and a merchant's sheet confirms.
The barrel regime of eight months apart and fifteen more blended rests on one review of the 2012; a second source confirms only ageing in oak in two steps, so the record keeps it to one vintage.
The founder is not named: no source found says he has died, and his family later left the house for a separate bodega, which rests on one source and is left out.
The present owner is volatile and is not named; a provincial plan of 1996 to irrigate the zone rests on one source and is told only as river water brought to the desert.
